name: Infrastructure item order with project code dictionaries
review_status: Derived from Hungarian workbooks in production use. The structure below states what those files state.
description: Rail and road bills prepared for a state developer follow a prescribed item order rather than a free structure, and the order is what the client's monitoring system reads. Each line carries a structure code that spells out its place in the work breakdown, a sequential row number, and an item number formed from the two that has to be unique inside the project. Alongside those sit tag columns, each one a code resolved against a dictionary shipped with the project, and the workbook carries its own check column per dictionary.

code_format.structure_code: the outline path joined with '+', for example 1+1+1+2
code_format.row_number: sequential, three digits, unique in the project
code_format.item_number: the row number and the catalogue item number joined with '_', for example 103_010 010
code_format.catalogue_item_number: six or seven digits, written closed up or with one space after the third digit

tag_dictionaries.resolves: which structure the line belongs to
the depreciation class of the resulting asset
the item number to a name and a unit
the schedule activity the line is executed under
the owner of the resulting asset
the funding source of the line

schedule_link: The work-process tag is the programme activity. Where the line carries a start and a finish, those are the activity's dates, which is what lets one export feed both the cost report and the progress report.
self_check_columns: The workbook carries a check column beside each dictionary-backed tag, holding whether the code was found in its dictionary. A delivered file has them all true, and that is the invariant an import should preserve.
